Denture Stability

Dentures Moving While Eating: Causes and Treatment Options

Understanding why dentures may slip or shift during meals, the factors that affect denture stability, and how professional assessment can help identify suitable solutions.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Denture & Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dentures are designed to restore the ability to chew and speak comfortably after tooth loss. For many patients, they provide a practical and effective means of replacing missing teeth and maintaining everyday oral function.

However, some denture wearers experience movement or slipping while eating — particularly when biting into firmer foods or chewing for extended periods. This instability can make mealtimes uncomfortable and may affect confidence when eating in social settings.

Denture movement during eating is a common concern, and it can develop gradually over time as the shape of the jawbone and gum tissues changes. Professional dental assessment can help determine why the dentures are moving and identify appropriate treatment options to improve stability and comfort.

Why Dentures May Move While Eating

Conventional dentures rely on the shape and contour of the gum tissue and underlying jawbone for support and retention. When the denture fits well and the supporting structures are intact, the denture is held in position by suction, muscle control, and the close adaptation of the denture base to the gum surface.

Over time, however, the jawbone naturally remodels following tooth loss — a process known as bone resorption. As the bone recedes, the ridge that supports the denture becomes flatter and narrower, reducing the surface area available for denture retention. This is particularly common in the lower jaw, where denture stability is often more difficult to achieve.

As these changes occur, the fit of the denture may become less precise, allowing movement during chewing or biting. The forces generated during eating can dislodge a denture that no longer fits securely, leading to slipping, rocking, or lifting away from the gum.

The degree of denture movement varies between individuals and depends on factors such as the extent of bone resorption, the type of denture, and the foods being eaten.

Common Causes of Denture Instability

Denture instability while eating is rarely caused by a single factor. In most cases, a combination of contributing elements affects how securely the denture sits during function.

Jawbone Shrinkage After Tooth Loss

Following tooth extraction, the jawbone gradually resorbs over time. This reduces the height and width of the ridge that supports the denture, compromising fit and retention — particularly in the lower jaw where bone loss tends to be more pronounced.

Changes in Gum Shape

The soft tissues that line the denture-bearing area can change in shape and volume over time. Weight changes, medication, and the natural ageing process may all contribute to alterations in gum contour, affecting the fit of the denture.

Ill-Fitting Dentures

Dentures that were not accurately fitted at the outset, or that have not been adjusted as the mouth has changed, may lack the close adaptation needed for stable retention. An imprecise fit allows movement under the forces of chewing.

Material Wear & Lower Jaw Challenges

Over years of use, denture materials can wear, warp, or develop surface irregularities that affect fit. The lower jaw presents particular challenges for denture stability due to the presence of the tongue and the typically flatter ridge, which offers less natural retention.

Signs Dentures Are Not Stable While Eating

Denture instability while eating may develop gradually, and patients sometimes adapt their eating habits without fully recognising the extent of the problem. The following signs may indicate that denture stability has been affected.

Slipping During Chewing

Dentures that shift, rock, or lift away from the gums while chewing may no longer fit securely enough to withstand normal bite forces.

Difficulty Biting Into Foods

Struggling to bite into firmer foods such as apples, crusty bread, or raw vegetables may indicate that the denture lacks adequate stability for incising.

Clicking or Shifting Sounds

Audible clicking or shifting of the denture during meals can be an indication of poor retention and may cause self-consciousness when eating in company.

Avoiding Certain Foods

Many patients with unstable dentures gradually restrict their diet, avoiding foods that are difficult to chew. Over time, this can affect nutritional intake and reduce enjoyment of meals.

Potential Effects on Oral Function

When dentures move during eating, the effects extend beyond simple inconvenience. Understanding the wider impact can help patients appreciate the value of seeking professional advice.

Chewing efficiency is often significantly affected. Unstable dentures cannot generate the same bite force as well-fitting ones, which means food may not be broken down as thoroughly. This can affect digestion and may lead patients to favour softer, less nutritious foods.

Food choices and diet tend to become more restricted over time. Patients may avoid fibrous vegetables, fresh fruit, nuts, and lean meats — foods that are important for maintaining a balanced diet and overall health.

Confidence when eating in social settings can also be affected. The worry that dentures may slip or make noise during a meal can cause anxiety and lead some patients to avoid eating in public altogether.

Additionally, dentures that move excessively can place uneven pressure on the gum tissues, potentially causing sore spots, irritation, and discomfort that further compounds the problem.

Treatment Options to Improve Denture Stability

Treatment for denture instability depends on clinical findings, including the condition of the denture, the health of the gum tissues, and the amount of jawbone support available.

Denture Adjustment or Replacement

If the existing denture has become ill-fitting due to changes in the mouth, adjustment or the fabrication of a new, better-fitting denture may help improve stability. Modern denture materials and techniques can achieve a more precise fit than older dentures.

Denture Relining

Relining involves adding new material to the fitting surface of the denture to improve its adaptation to the current shape of the gum ridge. This can be a practical option when the denture teeth are still in good condition but the fit has deteriorated.

Implant-Retained Dentures

For patients who continue to experience instability despite denture adjustments, implant-retained dentures may offer a more reliable solution. Dental implants placed in the jawbone provide secure attachment points for the denture, significantly reducing movement during eating and speaking.

Full Arch Implant Solutions

In cases of extensive tooth loss, All-on-4 dental implants or a full arch implant bridge may provide a fixed alternative to removable dentures. These solutions are supported entirely by dental implants and do not rely on gum suction for retention.

Options vary depending on bone support and denture condition. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

When Implant-Supported Dentures May Be Considered

Dental implants can provide a stable foundation for dentures by creating fixed attachment points within the jawbone. Unlike conventional dentures, which rest on the gum surface, implant-retained dentures clip or lock onto implants, providing considerably improved stability during chewing and speaking.

This approach may be particularly beneficial for lower denture wearers, where bone resorption often makes conventional denture retention especially challenging. Even a small number of implants can make a meaningful difference to denture stability and patient comfort.

Whether implant-supported dentures are suitable depends on a number of factors, including the health and volume of the available jawbone, overall medical health, and the patient's expectations and preferences. A comprehensive clinical evaluation, including dental imaging, is necessary to determine whether this treatment pathway is appropriate.

For patients seeking a fully fixed solution, full mouth reconstruction using implant-supported bridges may also be an option worth discussing during the assessment process.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Denture stability problems should be evaluated by a dental professional who can assess both the condition of the denture and the health of the underlying oral structures. A clinical examination can help identify the specific cause of the movement and determine the most appropriate course of action.

Assessment may involve checking the fit and adaptation of the denture, evaluating the shape and height of the ridge, and assessing the health of the gum tissues. Where implant-supported solutions are being considered, imaging such as cone beam CT scans may be required to evaluate bone volume and plan implant placement.

Treatment planning varies depending on individual needs. What works well for one patient may not be suitable for another, which is why personalised assessment is an essential first step.

Assessment and treatment planning for denture stability concerns are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options.
